newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian FinMin urges pyramid scheme control.
newsitem.headline: Albanian FinMin urges pyramid scheme control.

text.p: Albanian Finance Minister Arben Malaj pressed on Wednesday for quick adoption of a law to examine and regulate the pyramid investment schemes whose collapse pushed the Balkan nation to the brink of anarchy.
"We are not here to close companies, but we cannot turn a blind eye to their activity," Malaj told a press conference.
Widespread rioting shook Albania in February and March when five of the schemes collapsed, as people who had invested their life savings took to the streets.
Four other pyramid investment companies are still operating, but they have stopped paying interest.

Malaj, a Socialist in the nine-party National Reconciliation government, said the International Monetary Fund and World Bank wanted the law on pyramid schemes and the budget passed in order to continue scheduled projects in Albania.

"I regret the parliament has avoided voting for the bills so far," he said. The Albanian parliament is dominated by the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha, who is blamed by many of his countrymen for the collapse of the schemes.

Malaj denied his ministry planned to close down the rest of the schemes, saying the law envisaged the formation of a broad-based commission which would control the companies and cooperate with prosecutors investigating their activity.
Malaj said that any government that came to power after early elections due on June 29 would have to deal with the issue of returning the funds in the schemes that were still afloat.
He said the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (BERD) had agreed to provide credits to small Albanian companies hit by the collapse.
"It's about advantageous credits for companies brought near bankcruptcy, not recompense for the money lost in pyramid schemes," he said.
Malaj said it was also important to pass the budget, as the government was grabbling with a budget deficit of 55 billion leks ($400 million) and the devaluation of local lek currency.
"We hope the budget deficit will be reduced by 3 billion leks," he said, adding international humanitarian aid given after the unrest would bring in another one billion.
From late 1995, the budget deficit started to expand.

Spending by the Democratic Party government rose ahead of a general election in May 1996 and local elections in October. In 1996 the deficit rose to about 11 percent of GDP from only seven percent in 1995, and expected to be 15 percent in 1997.
Malaj said he wanted to inrease Value Added Tax (VAT) from 12.5 percent to 18 percent, and to drastically cut state spending.
"I know these measures are not popular, but even though I'm a Socialist, I'd prefer to undertake rightest steps in order to stop the decline of the economy " he said.
